\chapter{The Letters Themselves}
\label{ch:abecedario}
\hlchaptermodality{425}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name every letter of the Spanish alphabet, spell a name aloud over a telephone, tell b from v when somebody asks, and say where a word may and may not be broken.}

Spell a surname aloud letter by letter, say that a vowel carries its accent, and settle the b-or-v question the way a Spanish speaker does.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el abecedario]{el abecedario — twenty-seven letters, and one that English does not have}

\label{lesson:ES-C425-abecedario}



\begin{quote}
The last chapter gave you the marks that go between the letters. This chapter is about the letters themselves — which you have been reading for four hundred chapters and have never been asked to name.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el abecedario} — \textquotedblleft{}the alphabet.\textquotedblright{}

Look at the name: \textbf{a-be-ce-de}. It is the first four letters, read aloud and glued together. Spanish also says \textbf{el alfabeto}, from the Greek \emph{alpha} and \emph{beta} doing the identical trick in another language.

The Spanish alphabet has \textbf{twenty-seven} letters: the twenty-six of English, plus \textbf{ñ}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the letters, and what each is called}]
Knowing the shapes is not enough. To spell a name over a telephone you need the \textbf{names}, and most of them are not what an English speaker would guess:

The names are not a list to memorise. A letter is named by \textbf{putting a vowel beside its sound}, and there are only three patterns.

\textbf{The five vowels are called by their own sound}, and that is the whole rule for them: \emph{a, e, i, o, u}.

\textbf{Most consonants take an -e after}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{name} \\
\midrule
b, c, d & be, ce, de \\
g, p, t & ge, pe, te \\
v, y & uve, ye \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Five take an e- before instead}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{name} \\
\midrule
f, l & efe, ele \\
m, n & eme, ene \\
s & ese \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{And the leftovers have names of their own}, which are the ones to learn deliberately:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{name} \\
\midrule
h & hache \\
j & jota \\
k & ka \\
q & cu \\
r & erre \\
w & uve doble \\
x & equis \\
z & zeta \\
ñ & eñe \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Nine irregular names out of twenty-seven letters is a small thing to carry.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el abecedario\textquotedblright{}, and hear the four letters inside the word
  \item how many letters Spanish has (twenty-seven)
  \item the one Spanish has and English does not (\emph{eñe})
  \item the names of the letters in your own first name
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the word \emph{abecedario} come from? (The first four letters said aloud.) What is \textbf{h} called? (\emph{Hache}.) What is \textbf{j} called? (\emph{Jota}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[be larga o be corta]{be larga o be corta — the letters that needed a second name}

\label{lesson:ES-C425-dos-nombres}



\begin{quote}
Say the names of \textbf{b} and \textbf{v}. Now say the two letters out loud as sounds, and notice the problem you have created.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
In Spanish, \textbf{b} and \textbf{v} are pronounced \textbf{identically}. There is no \emph{v} sound in the language at all.

That is fine while you are speaking and a catastrophe while you are spelling. So Spanish grew extra names whose whole job is to tell the two apart:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{plain name} & \textbf{the disambiguating names} \\
\midrule
b & be & \textbf{be larga}, be alta, be grande \\
v & uve & \textbf{ve corta}, ve baja, ve chica \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Larga} and \emph{alta} describe the tall stem of \textbf{b}; \emph{corta} and \emph{baja} describe the short \textbf{v}. A Spanish speaker dictating an address will reach for these without thinking, and a listening paper will play them.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the other letters with two names}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{names} \\
\midrule
w & uve doble, doble ve, doble u \\
y & ye, i griega \\
z & zeta, ceta \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Y} is the interesting one. \emph{I griega} means \textquotedblleft{}Greek i\textquotedblright{} — the letter arrived from Greek \emph{upsilon} and Spanish named it after where it came from, while calling the ordinary \textbf{i} \emph{i latina} when it needs the contrast. The Academy now recommends \textbf{ye}, and both are in use.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{be larga} and \emph{ve corta}, and say which letter each one is
  \item why Spanish needed the second names at all
  \item the two names for \textbf{y}
  \item what \emph{i griega} literally means, and why
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Do \textbf{b} and \textbf{v} sound different in Spanish? (No — they are identical.) So what are \emph{be larga} and \emph{ve corta} for? (Telling the two apart when spelling aloud.) What does \emph{i griega} mean? (Greek i.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[las cinco vocales]{las cinco vocales — five letters, five sounds, and no exceptions}

\label{lesson:ES-C425-vocales}



\begin{quote}
Name the five vowels in Spanish. You have been saying them since the first chapter without being told they were a closed set.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{las cinco vocales} — \textquotedblleft{}the five vowels\textquotedblright{}: \textbf{a, e, i, o, u}.

\emph{Vocal} is from Latin \emph{vox}, \textquotedblleft{}voice\textquotedblright{} — a vowel is the part of a word you can actually sing. The same root gives \emph{voz}, \emph{vocabulario} and English \emph{vocal}.

Here is the part that makes Spanish kind to a reader: \textbf{each of the five has one sound, and it keeps it.} English \emph{a} is different in \emph{cat}, \emph{car}, \emph{cake} and \emph{about}. Spanish \emph{a} is the same in every word that has ever been written.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the two marks a vowel can carry}]
Only vowels take marks in Spanish, and there are exactly two:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{mark} & \textbf{name} & \textbf{what it does} \\
\midrule
á é í ó ú & la tilde, el acento & marks which syllable is stressed \\
ü & la diéresis & makes a silent \textbf{u} speak \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{La tilde} never changes the sound of the vowel — it only says \emph{stress this one}. That is why it can tell two identical words apart: \emph{el} is \emph{the}, \emph{él} is \emph{he}; \emph{si} is \emph{if}, \emph{sí} is \emph{yes}.

\textbf{La diéresis} appears on \textbf{ü} and nowhere else. In \emph{guerra} the \textbf{u} is silent; in \emph{pingüino} the two dots say \emph{pronounce me}. Two dots, one job.

Note the vocabulary trap: Spanish \emph{tilde} means the \textbf{accent mark}. The squiggle over \textbf{ñ} is \emph{la virgulilla}, and English calls that one the tilde. The two languages use the word for different marks.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the five vowels in order
  \item the difference between \emph{el} and \emph{él}, and what the mark is doing
  \item \emph{pingüino}, and say what the two dots are for
  \item how many sounds Spanish \textbf{a} has (one)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{la tilde} do to the sound of a vowel? (Nothing — it marks stress.) Which letter carries \emph{la diéresis}? (Only \textbf{ü}.) In Spanish, is \emph{tilde} the mark on \textbf{ñ}? (No — that is \emph{la virgulilla}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[los dígrafos]{los dígrafos — two letters, one sound, and a change made in 1994}

\label{lesson:ES-C425-digrafos}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{chico}, \emph{llave} and \emph{perro}. Each of those has two identical or paired letters doing a single job. Name how many sounds the doubled part makes.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{un dígrafo} — \textquotedblleft{}a digraph\textquotedblright{}: \textbf{two letters that spell one sound.}

Greek \emph{di-} two + \emph{graphē} writing. Spanish has five:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{digraph} & \textbf{example} & \textbf{one sound} \\
\midrule
ch & chico & as in English \emph{church} \\
ll & llave & a \emph{y} sound for most speakers \\
rr & perro & the long rolled r \\
gu & guerra & a hard \textbf{g}, with the \textbf{u} silent \\
qu & queso & a \textbf{k}, with the \textbf{u} silent \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The last two are the ones that catch a reader out. In \emph{guerra} and \emph{queso} the \textbf{u} is \textbf{not pronounced}. It is there to keep the \textbf{g} and \textbf{c} hard in front of \textbf{e} and \textbf{i} — which is exactly why \emph{pingüino} needs the two dots to cancel the silence.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the 1994 change, and why a dictionary moved}]
\textbf{Ch} and \textbf{ll} used to be letters of the alphabet in their own right, with their own names (\emph{che}, \emph{elle}) and their own sections in a dictionary. \emph{Chico} came after every word beginning with \textbf{c}, not inside them.

In 1994 they stopped being separate letters. A dictionary printed before then and one printed after put the same word in a different place:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{before 1994} & \textbf{after} \\
\midrule
chico & its own \textbf{ch} section & under \textbf{c} \\
llave & its own \textbf{ll} section & under \textbf{l} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

They are still digraphs and still spell one sound. What changed is only how they are \textbf{filed}. If you use an older Spanish dictionary and cannot find a word, this is usually why.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the five digraphs
  \item \emph{guerra} and \emph{queso}, and say what the \textbf{u} is doing in each (nothing audible — it keeps the first letter hard)
  \item where you would look up \emph{chico} in a dictionary printed today
  \item why \emph{pingüino} needs the two dots
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many sounds does a digraph spell? (One.) Is the \textbf{u} of \emph{queso} pronounced? (No.) What happened to \textbf{ch} and \textbf{ll} in 1994? (They stopped being separate letters of the alphabet and are filed under \textbf{c} and \textbf{l}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la sílaba]{la sílaba — what you may break, and what you may not}

\label{lesson:ES-C425-silabas}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{chico} slowly, in pieces. Say where you would break it if the line ran out — and note that the answer cannot be between the \textbf{c} and the \textbf{h}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la sílaba} — \textquotedblleft{}the syllable.\textquotedblright{} Greek \emph{syllab\'{\={e}}}, \textquotedblleft{}a taking together\textquotedblright{} — letters taken together into one beat.

When a word will not fit at the end of a line, Spanish breaks it \textbf{between syllables} and marks the break with \emph{el guion}. What matters for a written paper is which groups may \textbf{never} be split:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{never split} & \textbf{because} \\
\midrule
ch, ll, rr, gu, qu & each is one sound \\
a consonant + l or r & \emph{bl, br, cl, cr, pl, pr, tr…} hold together \\
a diphthong & two vowels in one beat stay in it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{chi-co}, never \emph{c-hico}. \emph{Ha-blar}, never \emph{hab-lar}. \emph{Pe-rro}, never \emph{per-ro}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: words Spanish spells two ways}]
A small set of words has two accepted spellings, and an exam will not mark either wrong:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{both accepted} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
sicología & psicología \\
setiembre & septiembre \\
quiosco & kiosco \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The pattern is a \textbf{simplified} form beside the older one that keeps a consonant cluster the language stopped pronouncing. Spanish spelling follows the mouth more closely than English does, so when a cluster goes quiet the spelling is eventually allowed to follow.

One last rule a form actually tests: \textbf{a number written in figures is never split across a line.} \emph{2026} stays whole.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item where \emph{hablar} may be broken (\emph{ha-blar})
  \item why \emph{chico} cannot be broken between \textbf{c} and \textbf{h}
  \item two accepted spellings of the word for September
  \item whether a year in figures may be split (no)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does Greek \emph{syllab\'{\={e}}} mean? (A taking together.) May \emph{br} be split? (No.) Is \emph{sicología} a spelling mistake? (No — both spellings are accepted.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[veintisiete letras]{veintisiete letras — the whole set, sorted three ways}

\label{lesson:ES-C425-repaso-letras}



\begin{quote}
Say how many letters Spanish has, and name the one English lacks.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what you now know about each group}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{group} & \textbf{the useful fact} \\
\midrule
the five vowels & one sound each, and it never varies \\
most consonants & named by adding \textbf{-e}, or \textbf{e-} in front \\
nine consonants & have names of their own to learn \\
five digraphs & two letters, one sound \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And the marks, which only vowels take:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{mark} & \textbf{on} & \textbf{job} \\
\midrule
la tilde & any vowel & marks the stressed syllable \\
la diéresis & only \textbf{ü} & makes a silent \textbf{u} speak \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the three things that stop a line break}]
A break may fall between syllables but never inside:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a \textbf{digraph} — \emph{chi-co}, not \emph{c-hico}
  \item a consonant plus \textbf{l} or \textbf{r} — \emph{ha-blar}, not \emph{hab-lar}
  \item a \textbf{diphthong}, or a number in figures
\end{itemize}

Those three cover nearly everything a written paper can test, and all three come from one idea: \textbf{do not break what is said in one beat.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the nine letters with names of their own
  \item the five digraphs
  \item the two names for \textbf{b} and the two for \textbf{v}, and why they exist
  \item three places a line may not be broken
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does Spanish need \emph{be larga} and \emph{ve corta}? (\textbf{B} and \textbf{v} sound identical.) How many sounds does a digraph spell? (One.) What single idea governs where a line may break? (Do not break what is said in one beat.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¿Cómo se escribe?]{¿Cómo se escribe? — the task the letter names are for}

\label{lesson:ES-C425-sintesis-deletreo}



\begin{quote}
Somebody on a telephone asks how your surname is written. Spell it aloud in Spanish before reading on.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the question, and what it is not}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{question} & \textbf{what it asks for} \\
\midrule
¿Cómo se escribe? & how it is \textbf{written} — spell it \\
¿Cómo se dice? & how it is \textbf{said} — the word itself \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A form-filling exchange uses the first. An exam's listening paper uses it to dictate a name at you letter by letter, which is the one situation where knowing \emph{hache} and \emph{jota} and \emph{equis} is the difference between hearing a name and writing it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Read this exchange aloud:

\begin{quote}
— ¿Cómo se escribe su apellido? — Vázquez. Uve, a con tilde, zeta, cu, u, e, zeta. — ¿Uve o be? — Uve. Ve corta.
\end{quote}

The last two turns are the reason the second names exist. The listener could not tell \textbf{b} from \textbf{v} by ear, asked, and got an answer that settles it.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿Cómo se escribe?\textquotedblright{}
  \item your own first name, letter by letter, in Spanish
  \item how you would say that a letter carries a written accent (\emph{con tilde})
  \item how you would settle it if somebody could not tell your \textbf{b} from a \textbf{v}
  \item where your surname would break if it ran off the end of a line, and name one group inside it that may not be split
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which question asks for a spelling rather than a word? (\emph{¿Cómo se escribe?}) How do you say that a vowel carries its accent mark? (\emph{Con tilde}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
